newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba-total, not structural, deficit is decisive.
newsitem.headline: Buba-total, not structural, deficit is decisive.

text.p: The German Bundesbank on Wednesday presented a model for assessing the structural components of a country's budget deficit, but warned that governments must continue to focus on the total shortfall.

In its April monthly report, the Bundesbank said its study showed that a worsening of 3-1/3 percentage points in Germany's deficit position between 1989 and 1996 was attributable to non-cyclical factors, such as higher debt servicing.
But it warned against overweighting such structural deficit calculations in the formulation of policy.

"Narrowing one's view to consider only the structural deficit brings with it the danger of underestimating the extent of a mistake on the fiscal poicy front, particularly as the methods and statistical problems in calculating structural deficits have so far led to very different results or interpretations," the Bundesbank said.
"The financial total balance of state activities must remain the decisive measurement -- due also to its relevance for borrowing needs," the Bundesbank said.

It added that the overall figure was also the basis for assessing countries' qualification for monetary union under the terms of the Maastricht treaty and for countries' later adherence to the stability act on fiscal discipline.

"According to the Maastricht treaty, this is the measure which should be used as a basis for the examination of the question of whether the fiscal policy debt criterion is reached," the Bundesbank said.

Under the terms of the Maastricht treaty, states which want to join a single currency in 1999 must be running a budget deficit of no more than a reference level of three percent of gross domestic product.
Germany, in common with many other European states, is facing serious problems in reining in its deficit to meet the criteria.

Economic weakness over the last few years in Europe has led some to argue that the structural deficit, and not the overall deficit which may be exaggerated by economic weakness, should be used as the basis for the Maastricht assessment.
